questions.question: Why does the direct reaction of ammonia with 1-bromobutane yield a messy mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary ammonium salts?

options.label: A
options.text: The primary amine product (butylamine) is a stronger nucleophile than ammonia due to the electron-donating alkyl group, competing for remaining alkyl halide.

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate.

options.label: C
options.text: Ammonia is insoluble in organic solvents.

options.label: D
options.text: Butylamine decomposes into butene and nitrogen.

questions.correct_answer: The primary amine product (butylamine) is a stronger nucleophile than ammonia due to the electron-donating alkyl group, competing for remaining alkyl halide.
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups increase nitrogen nucleophilicity by inductive donation, causing mono-alkylated amines to react faster than ammonia.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis Clean Primary Amine Mechanism
questions.question: Why does the Gabriel synthesis using potassium phthalimide prevent polyalkylation?

options.label: A
options.text: Phthalimide reacts via an E2 mechanism exclusively.

options.label: B
options.text: The hydrazine cleavage step removes extra alkyl groups.

options.label: C
options.text: The phthalimide anion can only alkylate once because the resulting N-alkylphthalimide has no remaining acidic protons or basic nucleophilic sites on nitrogen.

options.label: D
options.text: Phthalimide is an oxidizer that destroys secondary amines.

questions.correct_answer: The phthalimide anion can only alkylate once because the resulting N-alkylphthalimide has no remaining acidic protons or basic nucleophilic sites on nitrogen.
questions.explanation: Phthalimide serves as a protected nitrogen synthon with exactly one nucleophilic lone pair, guaranteeing monoalkylation.

questions.question: Why is sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH₃CN) at pH 6 uniquely suited for reductive amination of ketones?

options.label: A
options.text: NaBH₃CN precipitates all unreacted amines.

options.label: B
options.text: The electron-withdrawing cyano group attenuates hydride reactivity so that NaBH₃CN selectively reduces protonated iminium ions (formed at pH 6) while ignoring neutral ketones.

options.label: C
options.text: NaBH₃CN only reduces aromatic rings.

options.label: D
options.text: NaBH₃CN is a powerful oxidizer.

questions.correct_answer: The electron-withdrawing cyano group attenuates hydride reactivity so that NaBH₃CN selectively reduces protonated iminium ions (formed at pH 6) while ignoring neutral ketones.
questions.explanation: At pH 6, the iminium cation [R₂C=N⁺HR'] is protonated and far more electrophilic than the parent ketone, allowing selective reduction by mild NaBH₃CN.

questions.question: Why does thermal elimination of quaternary ammonium hydroxides (Hofmann elimination) yield the less substituted alkene?

options.label: A
options.text: The less substituted alkene is thermodynamically more stable.

options.label: B
options.text: The bulky -N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group creates severe steric crowding in the transition state, forcing base to abstract the more accessible, less hindered β-hydrogen.

options.label: C
options.text: Quaternary amines are weak leaving groups.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a planar carbocation intermediate.

questions.correct_answer: The bulky -N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group creates severe steric crowding in the transition state, forcing base to abstract the more accessible, less hindered β-hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Steric clash between the bulky trialkylammonium group and the base enforces deprotonation at the least hindered methyl position (Hofmann rule).

questions.question: How is the active electrophile (NO⁺, nitrosonium ion) generated during diazotization of aniline with NaNO₂ and HCl?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrite is protonated to nitrous acid (HONO), which is protonated again to H₂O⁺-NO and loses water to generate the electrophilic nitrosonium cation (⁺N=O).

options.label: B
options.text: Hydrochloric acid cleaves aniline into nitrogen gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium nitrite undergoes homolytic cleavage.

options.label: D
options.text: Nitrite is oxidized by air to nitrate.

questions.correct_answer: Nitrite is protonated to nitrous acid (HONO), which is protonated again to H₂O⁺-NO and loses water to generate the electrophilic nitrosonium cation (⁺N=O).
questions.explanation: Acid-promoted dehydration of nitrous acid generates the reactive nitrosonium electrophile (NO⁺) that is attacked by the amine nitrogen.

questions.question: What is the mechanistic classification of the coupling reaction between benzenediazonium chloride and 2-naphthol?

options.label: A
options.text: Diels-Alder cycloaddition.

options.label: B
options.text: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr).

options.label: C
options.text: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) where the diazonium cation acts as a weak electrophile attacking the highly activated, electron-rich naphthol ring.

options.label: D
options.text: Free radical coupling.

questions.correct_answer: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) where the diazonium cation acts as a weak electrophile attacking the highly activated, electron-rich naphthol ring.
questions.explanation: The diazonium ion (Ar-N₂⁺) is a weak electrophile that undergoes EAS exclusively with strongly activated aromatic rings (phenols and arylamines).

questions.question: What is the mechanistic pathway for the conversion of an aryldiazonium tetrafluoroborate salt to an aryl fluoride upon heating?

options.label: A
options.text: Thermal decomposition expels N₂ gas to generate an unstable aryl cation, which instantly captures fluoride from the BF₄⁻ counterion: Ar-N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ → Ar-F + N₂ + BF₃.

options.label: B
options.text: Homolytic radical fluorination by elemental F₂.

options.label: C
options.text: Addition of BF₃ across the aromatic π bonds.

options.label: D
options.text: Direct SN2 displacement of N₂ by fluoride in solution.

questions.correct_answer: Thermal decomposition expels N₂ gas to generate an unstable aryl cation, which instantly captures fluoride from the BF₄⁻ counterion: Ar-N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ → Ar-F + N₂ + BF₃.
questions.explanation: Thermal pyrolysis of the diazonium fluoroborate proceeds through an aryl cation intermediate that abstracts fluoride from the complex anion.

questions.question: What is the role of hypophosphorous acid (H₃PO₂) in the synthetic deamination of aryldiazonium salts?

options.label: A
options.text: H₃PO₂ acts as a mild hydride/radical reducing agent, replacing the diazonium group with hydrogen and releasing N₂ gas, H₃PO₃, and HCl.

options.label: B
options.text: H₃PO₂ precipitates the diazonium salt as an explosive solid.

options.label: C
options.text: H₃PO₂ converts the diazonium salt to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: D
options.text: H₃PO₂ oxidizes the diazonium salt to a nitro compound.

questions.correct_answer: H₃PO₂ acts as a mild hydride/radical reducing agent, replacing the diazonium group with hydrogen and releasing N₂ gas, H₃PO₃, and HCl.
questions.explanation: H₃PO₂ reduces the diazonium group to a C-H bond, enabling amino groups to be used as temporary directing/activating groups and then removed.

questions.topic: Amide Reduction to Amine Aluminate Intermediate
questions.question: Why does LiAlH₄ reduce amides to amines rather than alcohols (unlike esters)?

options.label: A
options.text: Amines are oxidizers that prevent alcohol formation.

options.label: B
options.text: Amides are converted to acyl chlorides in situ.

options.label: C
options.text: The C-N bond is broken first by hydride.

options.label: D
options.text: The oxygen atom of the tetrahedral intermediate coordinates strongly to aluminum as a good aluminate leaving group, expelling O-Al to form an iminium ion that is reduced to amine.

questions.correct_answer: The oxygen atom of the tetrahedral intermediate coordinates strongly to aluminum as a good aluminate leaving group, expelling O-Al to form an iminium ion that is reduced to amine.
questions.explanation: Oxygen has higher affinity for aluminum than nitrogen; the C-O bond is cleaved to form an iminium intermediate that is reduced to the amine.

questions.topic: Amine Protection as Acetamide for Bromination
questions.question: Why must aniline be converted to acetanilide prior to monobromination with Br₂?

options.label: A
options.text: The free amino group is too strongly activating, causing uncontrollable tribromination (2,4,6-tribromoaniline); the acetamido group moderates activation via resonance into its own carbonyl.

options.label: B
options.text: Aniline oxidizes Br₂ to bromate.

options.label: C
options.text: Aniline is insoluble in bromine water.

options.label: D
options.text: Aniline reacts with Br₂ to form nitrogen tribromide.

questions.correct_answer: The free amino group is too strongly activating, causing uncontrollable tribromination (2,4,6-tribromoaniline); the acetamido group moderates activation via resonance into its own carbonyl.
questions.explanation: Acetylation moderates nitrogen lone pair donation into the ring by competing resonance with the carbonyl, enabling clean monobromination.

options.text: Amines are oxidizers that prevent alcohol formation.

options.label: B
options.text: Amides are converted to acyl chlorides in situ.

options.label: C
options.text: The oxygen atom of the tetrahedral intermediate coordinates strongly to aluminum as a good aluminate leaving group, expelling O-Al to form an iminium ion that is reduced to amine.

options.label: D
options.text: The C-N bond is broken first by hydride.

questions.correct_answer: The oxygen atom of the tetrahedral intermediate coordinates strongly to aluminum as a good aluminate leaving group, expelling O-Al to form an iminium ion that is reduced to amine.
questions.explanation: Oxygen has higher affinity for aluminum than nitrogen; the C-O bond is cleaved to form an iminium intermediate that is reduced to the amine.

questions.topic: Amine Protection as Acetamide for Bromination
questions.question: Why must aniline be converted to acetanilide prior to monobromination with Br₂?

options.label: A
options.text: Aniline reacts with Br₂ to form nitrogen tribromide.

options.label: B
options.text: Aniline is insoluble in bromine water.

options.label: C
options.text: Aniline oxidizes Br₂ to bromate.

options.label: D
options.text: The free amino group is too strongly activating, causing uncontrollable tribromination (2,4,6-tribromoaniline); the acetamido group moderates activation via resonance into its own carbonyl.

questions.correct_answer: The free amino group is too strongly activating, causing uncontrollable tribromination (2,4,6-tribromoaniline); the acetamido group moderates activation via resonance into its own carbonyl.
questions.explanation: Acetylation moderates nitrogen lone pair donation into the ring by competing resonance with the carbonyl, enabling clean monobromination.

questions.question: Why does the direct reaction of ammonia with 1-bromobutane yield a messy mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary ammonium salts?

options.label: A
options.text: Ammonia is insoluble in organic solvents.

options.label: B
options.text: Butylamine decomposes into butene and nitrogen.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate.

options.label: D
options.text: The primary amine product (butylamine) is a stronger nucleophile than ammonia due to the electron-donating alkyl group, competing for remaining alkyl halide.

questions.correct_answer: The primary amine product (butylamine) is a stronger nucleophile than ammonia due to the electron-donating alkyl group, competing for remaining alkyl halide.
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups increase nitrogen nucleophilicity by inductive donation, causing mono-alkylated amines to react faster than ammonia.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis Clean Primary Amine Mechanism
questions.question: Why does the Gabriel synthesis using potassium phthalimide prevent polyalkylation?

options.label: A
options.text: The phthalimide anion can only alkylate once because the resulting N-alkylphthalimide has no remaining acidic protons or basic nucleophilic sites on nitrogen.

options.label: B
options.text: The hydrazine cleavage step removes extra alkyl groups.

options.label: C
options.text: Phthalimide is an oxidizer that destroys secondary amines.

options.label: D
options.text: Phthalimide reacts via an E2 mechanism exclusively.

questions.correct_answer: The phthalimide anion can only alkylate once because the resulting N-alkylphthalimide has no remaining acidic protons or basic nucleophilic sites on nitrogen.
questions.explanation: Phthalimide serves as a protected nitrogen synthon with exactly one nucleophilic lone pair, guaranteeing monoalkylation.

questions.question: Why is sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH₃CN) at pH 6 uniquely suited for reductive amination of ketones?

options.label: A
options.text: NaBH₃CN precipitates all unreacted amines.

options.label: B
options.text: NaBH₃CN is a powerful oxidizer.

options.label: C
options.text: NaBH₃CN only reduces aromatic rings.

options.label: D
options.text: The electron-withdrawing cyano group attenuates hydride reactivity so that NaBH₃CN selectively reduces protonated iminium ions (formed at pH 6) while ignoring neutral ketones.

questions.correct_answer: The electron-withdrawing cyano group attenuates hydride reactivity so that NaBH₃CN selectively reduces protonated iminium ions (formed at pH 6) while ignoring neutral ketones.
questions.explanation: At pH 6, the iminium cation [R₂C=N⁺HR'] is protonated and far more electrophilic than the parent ketone, allowing selective reduction by mild NaBH₃CN.

questions.question: Why does thermal elimination of quaternary ammonium hydroxides (Hofmann elimination) yield the less substituted alkene?

options.label: A
options.text: The bulky -N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group creates severe steric crowding in the transition state, forcing base to abstract the more accessible, less hindered β-hydrogen.

options.label: B
options.text: Quaternary amines are weak leaving groups.

options.label: C
options.text: The less substituted alkene is thermodynamically more stable.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a planar carbocation intermediate.

questions.correct_answer: The bulky -N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group creates severe steric crowding in the transition state, forcing base to abstract the more accessible, less hindered β-hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Steric clash between the bulky trialkylammonium group and the base enforces deprotonation at the least hindered methyl position (Hofmann rule).

questions.question: How is the active electrophile (NO⁺, nitrosonium ion) generated during diazotization of aniline with NaNO₂ and HCl?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrite is oxidized by air to nitrate.

options.label: B
options.text: Hydrochloric acid cleaves aniline into nitrogen gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium nitrite undergoes homolytic cleavage.

options.label: D
options.text: Nitrite is protonated to nitrous acid (HONO), which is protonated again to H₂O⁺-NO and loses water to generate the electrophilic nitrosonium cation (⁺N=O).

questions.correct_answer: Nitrite is protonated to nitrous acid (HONO), which is protonated again to H₂O⁺-NO and loses water to generate the electrophilic nitrosonium cation (⁺N=O).
questions.explanation: Acid-promoted dehydration of nitrous acid generates the reactive nitrosonium electrophile (NO⁺) that is attacked by the amine nitrogen.

questions.question: What is the mechanistic classification of the coupling reaction between benzenediazonium chloride and 2-naphthol?

options.label: A
options.text: Free radical coupling.

options.label: B
options.text: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr).

options.label: C
options.text: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) where the diazonium cation acts as a weak electrophile attacking the highly activated, electron-rich naphthol ring.

options.label: D
options.text: Diels-Alder cycloaddition.

questions.correct_answer: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) where the diazonium cation acts as a weak electrophile attacking the highly activated, electron-rich naphthol ring.
questions.explanation: The diazonium ion (Ar-N₂⁺) is a weak electrophile that undergoes EAS exclusively with strongly activated aromatic rings (phenols and arylamines).

questions.question: What is the mechanistic pathway for the conversion of an aryldiazonium tetrafluoroborate salt to an aryl fluoride upon heating?

options.label: A
options.text: Addition of BF₃ across the aromatic π bonds.

options.label: B
options.text: Homolytic radical fluorination by elemental F₂.

options.label: C
options.text: Direct SN2 displacement of N₂ by fluoride in solution.

options.label: D
options.text: Thermal decomposition expels N₂ gas to generate an unstable aryl cation, which instantly captures fluoride from the BF₄⁻ counterion: Ar-N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ → Ar-F + N₂ + BF₃.

questions.correct_answer: Thermal decomposition expels N₂ gas to generate an unstable aryl cation, which instantly captures fluoride from the BF₄⁻ counterion: Ar-N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ → Ar-F + N₂ + BF₃.
questions.explanation: Thermal pyrolysis of the diazonium fluoroborate proceeds through an aryl cation intermediate that abstracts fluoride from the complex anion.

questions.question: What is the role of hypophosphorous acid (H₃PO₂) in the synthetic deamination of aryldiazonium salts?

options.label: A
options.text: H₃PO₂ precipitates the diazonium salt as an explosive solid.

options.label: B
options.text: H₃PO₂ converts the diazonium salt to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: C
options.text: H₃PO₂ oxidizes the diazonium salt to a nitro compound.

options.label: D
options.text: H₃PO₂ acts as a mild hydride/radical reducing agent, replacing the diazonium group with hydrogen and releasing N₂ gas, H₃PO₃, and HCl.

questions.correct_answer: H₃PO₂ acts as a mild hydride/radical reducing agent, replacing the diazonium group with hydrogen and releasing N₂ gas, H₃PO₃, and HCl.
questions.explanation: H₃PO₂ reduces the diazonium group to a C-H bond, enabling amino groups to be used as temporary directing/activating groups and then removed.
